subtype: Approach: decide which tasks the tool should and should not do [Thinking]
passage:
Day 1. Vasudha, in her final year, wrote three lines in her project notebook and taped them above her desk. AI may explain a concept I don't follow. AI may check my grammar. AI may not write my analysis. She thought: if I decide what the tool is for before I open it, I won't drift.

Day 4. At one in the morning, tired, she opened the tool and felt the pull to ask it for the whole results section. She read the taped lines, closed the window, and asked it instead to explain what a confidence interval means. Then she wrote the paragraph herself.

Day 9. Her classmate Pranav asked, "Can I see your prompt for the analysis?" Vasudha laughed. "I don't have one. I have a rule." She showed him the paper on the wall.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha put her three rules?
qa.a: She taped them above her desk.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling at one in the morning when she felt the pull to ask for the results section?
qa.a: Vasudha was tired and tempted, but her reading the rules and closing the window shows a determination to keep the work her own.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do if she was ever unsure whether a request fits her rules, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could ask whether the tool would be doing the thinking or helping her understand, because the purpose of the request decides whether it belongs.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Vasudha's rule?
qa.a: Pranav may find it a surprisingly simple answer, and could be prompted to think about what he wants the tool to do for him.

grounding: A final-year student sets a rule that AI may explain and check grammar but not write the analysis, choosing the purpose first.

passage:
Sit down, Bhupen, you asked how I got through my final year without letting the chatbot do everything. It wasn't wisdom. It was one bad night.
I was Madhav the last-minute man then. Farhan, my roommate, had the tool write his whole lab report, and I was tempted. But I opened my own data first and thought, what is this project actually for? If the tool writes the analysis, then the marks are for its thinking, not mine. And in the viva, who answers?
So I wrote three lines on a sticky note above my desk. The tool may explain a concept I'm stuck on. The tool may check my grammar. The tool may not write the analysis I submit.
Three months later, the external examiner asked why I chose that test. I could answer. Farhan couldn't.

qa.q: What were the three lines on Madhav's sticky note?
qa.a: The tool may explain a concept, the tool may check grammar, and the tool may not write the analysis Madhav submits.

qa.q: Why did Madhav feel tempted that night, and what stopped it?
qa.a: Madhav felt tempted because Farhan had the tool write a whole lab report, but asking what the project was for made the shortcut feel like handing over the marks.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Opening the data first and asking whose thinking gets marked was the turning point, because it set the tool's role before any temptation took over.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt in the viva when he couldn't answer?
qa.a: Farhan probably felt exposed and embarrassed, because the report looked finished but the reasoning behind it was not his.

grounding: Shows a final-year student deciding in advance that the tool may explain and check grammar but may not write the submitted analysis.

passage:
The hostel Wi-Fi died at nine, two nights before Rehana's thesis analysis was due. She sat on the stairwell where one bar of signal reached, laptop balanced on her knees.
"Just paste the data in and ask it to write the discussion," Sharmila called from their doorway. "Everyone does."
Rehana looked at the blinking cursor. If it writes the discussion, what did I spend a year learning? She opened a note and typed before anything else: Allowed: explain methods I don't get. Check grammar at the end. Not allowed: writing any sentence of my findings.
Then she asked the tool one question: why use a paired test here? The answer took ten minutes to load. She read it twice, closed the tab, and wrote her own paragraph by torchlight when the laptop dimmed. It was slow, but every line was hers.

qa.q: Where did Rehana sit when the Wi-Fi went down?
qa.a: She sat on the stairwell where one bar of signal reached.

qa.q: What was Rehana thinking as she looked at the cursor, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She felt torn and a little uneasy, wondering what her year of learning was worth if the tool wrote the discussion for her.

qa.q: What else could Rehana do to cope with the slow connection and still keep her rule?
qa.a: She could write her discussion offline first and save grammar checks for later, so the weak signal is used only for small questions.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see Rehana's choice?
qa.a: Sharmila may think Rehana is making the night harder than it needs to be, since in Sharmila's view everyone lets the tool write.

grounding: Shows a final-year student setting the tool's purpose first: explaining and grammar help, but no writing of the submitted analysis, under time pressure.
